newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain employers, unions in preliminary accord.
newsitem.headline: Spain employers, unions in preliminary accord.

text.p: Spain's unions and employers reached a preliminary agreement on Wednesday that will lay the ground for a final accord on crucial labour reforms.
After weeks of intense talks, unions and employers said they were ready to draft an agreement aimed at easing Spain's towering unemployment -- the highest in Europe at just under 22 percent.

"Today we have come close enough in our positions to give us sufficient basis to become more concrete and put things down on paper," Antonio Gutierrez, head of the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) union told a news conference.
While the two sides would not expand on the exact contents of a final deal, they said they had reached broad agreements on permanent contracts, dismissal terms and collective negotiation.
The government had given unions and employers until early March to reach a deal before it stepped in and forced its own measures.
On Wednesday, it appeared to be becoming impatient.
"The government wants an agreement to be reached this week, and if it is today, all the better," Labour Minister Javier Arenas told reporters before entering Congress.
After a five-day break in talks, unions set the ground for an agreement on Wednesday with a fresh proposal. Local media said employers had agreed to the terms of the offer.
Unions had proposed a new contract which met their demand for greater stability and sought to placate employers with lower unfair dismissal costs.
Unions have been demanding the creation of a more secure contract, especially for youths who suffer most from unemployment in Spain.
Employers, meanwhile, are keen to see dismissal costs cut. They complain Spain's severance pay is by far the highest in the European Union and dissuades them from hiring staff.

While the exact dismissal costs of the proposed contract remained vague, unions said they would be below the current level of 45 days per year worked. Local media said the level agreed had been around 30 days.
The new contract applies to young workers, especially those seeking their first jobs, the long-term unemployed and temporary workers.
Employers association (CEOE) head Jose Maria Cuevas said representatives from the two sides would start to draft the agreement on Wednesday afternoon and could take some days.
The agreement will seek to ease the transition of youth workers into the labour market and attempt to abate Spain's problems with temporary contracts.
In 1996 less than five percent of new jobs were on permanent contracts.
